basic_information.name: US State AI Laws Patchwork (Colorado, California, Illinois, New York, Texas, Utah, and others)
basic_information.jurisdiction: US (state-level, across all 50 states — no comprehensive federal AI law exists)
basic_information.status: enacted — multiple state laws already in force (Utah AI Policy Act since May 2024, Illinois HB 3773 since January 2026, Texas TRAIGA since January 2026); others taking effect soon (Colorado SB 24-205 on June 30, 2026, NY RAISE Act on January 1, 2027). Over 1,200 AI bills introduced in 2025 alone, with 145 enacted. Legislative activity continues to accelerate in 2026.
basic_information.effective_date: Varies by state. Key dates: Utah AI Policy Act (SB 149) — May 1, 2024; Colorado AI Act (SB 24-205) — June 30, 2026 (delayed from February 1, 2026); California TFAIA (SB 53) — January 1, 2026; California AB 2013 — signed September 28, 2024; Illinois HB 3773 — January 1, 2026; Texas TRAIGA (HB 149) — January 1, 2026; New York RAISE Act — January 1, 2027.
basic_information.regulatory_philosophy: patchwork_federalism — In the absence of comprehensive federal AI legislation, US states are independently crafting AI regulations reflecting their own policy priorities. The result is a fragmented landscape where Colorado prioritizes algorithmic discrimination prevention, California focuses on frontier model safety and transparency, Illinois targets employment discrimination, Texas emphasizes innovation-friendly governance with safe harbors, and Utah takes a minimal-disclosure approach. No single state has adopted a comprehensive horizontal approach like the EU AI Act; most target specific domains (employment, consumer protection, frontier models) or specific harms (discrimination, deepfakes, child safety).

scope_and_content.summary: US state AI regulation constitutes a rapidly growing patchwork of laws addressing AI governance in the absence of comprehensive federal legislation. Key landmark laws include: Colorado's SB 24-205 (first comprehensive state AI law targeting algorithmic discrimination in high-risk AI systems), California's SB 53 (frontier AI model safety and transparency), California's AB 2013 (training data transparency), Illinois' HB 3773 (AI in employment decisions), Texas' TRAIGA (prohibited AI uses and regulatory sandbox), Utah's SB 149 (first state AI disclosure law), and New York's RAISE Act (frontier model transparency and incident reporting). Together, these laws create overlapping and sometimes conflicting compliance obligations for companies operating across state lines.
key_provisions: COLORADO SB 24-205 (Colorado AI Act): Requires developers and deployers of high-risk AI systems (those making 'consequential decisions' about consumers) to use reasonable care to protect against algorithmic discrimination. Developers must provide deployers with system documentation and impact assessment materials. Deployers must implement risk management programs, complete impact assessments, annually review deployments, notify consumers of AI use, and allow consumers to correct incorrect personal data. Covers decisions about employment, education, financial services, healthcare, housing, insurance, legal services, and essential government services. Enforceable exclusively by the Colorado Attorney General; violations treated as deceptive trade practices under the Colorado Consumer Protection Act ($20,000 per violation per consumer/transaction).

CALIFORNIA SB 53 (Transparency in Frontier AI Act, signed Sept 29, 2025): Requires 'large frontier developers' (those training models using >10^26 FLOPS) to draft and publish safety protocols for managing catastrophic risk, publish transparency reports, report critical safety incidents to state regulators, and establish whistleblower protections. Defines catastrophic risk as potential to kill 50+ people via cyberattack, facilitate CBRN weapons, or cause >$1 billion in theft/damage. Civil penalties up to $1 million per violation enforced by the California AG. Includes robust whistleblower provisions with anti-retaliation protections.

CALIFORNIA AB 2013 (AI Training Data Transparency Act, signed Sept 28, 2024): Mandates that generative AI developers publish information about training datasets including sources, data types, whether copyrighted material is included, and collection timeframes.

CALIFORNIA SB 243 (Companion Chatbot Law): Requires operators of AI companion chatbots to disclose AI nature, maintain protocols to prevent suicidal ideation and self-harm content, and implement special protections for minors (including break reminders every three hours).

ILLINOIS HB 3773 (AI Employment Discrimination Act, signed Aug 9, 2024): Amends the Illinois Human Rights Act to prohibit employers from using AI in ways that discriminate against employees or applicants based on protected characteristics (including unintentional/disparate-impact discrimination). Requires employers to provide notice when AI is used in recruitment, hiring, promotions, and other employment decisions. Prohibits use of zip codes as proxy for protected classes. Enforced by Illinois Department of Human Rights; penalties up to $5,000 per violation plus back pay, reinstatement, and emotional distress damages.

TEXAS TRAIGA (HB 149, signed June 22, 2025): Prohibits AI systems intentionally designed to harm persons, engage in criminal activity, infringe constitutional rights, unlawfully discriminate, or produce CSAM. Uses an intent-based liability standard (disparate impact alone insufficient). Requires government entities to disclose AI interactions to consumers. Creates safe harbors for organizations substantially complying with NIST AI RMF or discovering violations through internal testing. Establishes a Texas AI Council and regulatory sandbox program. Enforced exclusively by the Texas AG; no private right of action.

UTAH AI POLICY ACT (SB 149, signed March 13, 2024): First state AI law in the US. Requires disclosure of generative AI use upon consumer request. Regulated professionals (e.g., physicians) must disclose AI use proactively at the start of interactions. Creates the Office of Artificial Intelligence Policy and a regulatory sandbox for AI experimentation. Penalties up to $2,500 per administrative violation, $5,000 per court/administrative order violation.

NEW YORK RAISE ACT (signed Dec 19, 2025): Requires frontier AI model developers to create and publish safety protocols, report incidents to the state within 72 hours, and comply with transparency obligations. Originally used compute-cost thresholds; chapter amendments (expected January 2026) replace these with a $500 million revenue threshold for covered developers. Penalties up to $1 million for first violation, $3 million for subsequent violations. Creates oversight office within Department of Financial Services. Enforceable only by NY Attorney General; effective January 1, 2027.

ADDITIONAL SECTOR-SPECIFIC LAWS: Multiple states have passed narrower laws targeting deepfakes in elections, AI in healthcare, AI-generated content labeling, and AI in insurance decisions. In 2025, 38 states passed at least one AI-related bill.
scope_and_content.risk_classification: No unified risk classification across states. Colorado comes closest with its 'high-risk AI system' definition: an AI system that 'makes, or is a substantial factor in making, a consequential decision' — decisions with 'material legal or similarly significant effect' on consumers' access to employment, education, financial services, healthcare, housing, insurance, legal services, or essential government services. California SB 53 uses a compute threshold (>10^26 FLOPS) to identify 'frontier models' posing catastrophic risk. Texas focuses on intentional harmful uses rather than risk categories. Illinois is sector-specific (employment only). Each state defines 'AI,' 'high-risk,' and 'consequential decisions' differently, creating definitional fragmentation that complicates compliance.
scope_and_content.covered_entities: Varies significantly by state. Colorado: 'developers' (those who build or substantially modify AI systems) and 'deployers' (those who use AI systems for consequential decisions about consumers). California SB 53: 'large frontier developers' (those training models >10^26 FLOPS). Illinois: employers who use AI in employment decisions. Texas: any person who develops or deploys AI in Texas or serves Texas residents. Utah: any person causing generative AI to interact with consumers in Utah. New York: developers of 'frontier models' meeting revenue thresholds ($500 million).
scope_and_content.sector_scope: No single uniform sectoral approach. Colorado: employment, education, financial/lending, healthcare, housing, insurance, legal services, government services. Illinois: employment only. California SB 53: horizontal (any frontier model posing catastrophic risk). California SB 243: AI companion chatbots (child safety). Texas: horizontal with focus on prohibited harmful uses. Utah: horizontal (any generative AI consumer interaction). New York: horizontal (frontier models regardless of sector). Additional state laws address specific sectors: elections (deepfakes), healthcare, insurance, and education.
scope_and_content.open_source_treatment: Colorado SB 24-205 is the most explicit: developers who release a general-purpose AI model under a free and open-source license, with publicly available model parameters (weights, architecture, usage information), are exempt from developer obligations — unless the model is deployed as a high-risk AI system. The developer bears the burden of proving the exemption applies. California SB 53 does not contain a specific open-source exemption; its compute threshold (>10^26 FLOPS) effectively limits applicability to a handful of large labs (likely including Meta/Llama). Texas TRAIGA focuses on intent-based prohibitions rather than developer/deployer duties, making the open-source distinction less relevant. The New York RAISE Act uses revenue thresholds ($500 million), which would generally exclude open-source-only organizations but capture large labs releasing open-weight models.
scope_and_content.extraterritorial_reach: Most state laws apply to any entity doing business with or affecting residents of that state, regardless of where the entity is headquartered. Colorado applies to developers and deployers whose AI systems make consequential decisions about Colorado consumers. California SB 53 applies to developers training models above the compute threshold who serve California residents. Texas applies to anyone who 'promotes, advertises, or conducts business' in Texas or offers products/services to Texas residents. This creates de facto national reach for major AI providers who serve customers in all 50 states, effectively requiring compliance with the strictest state requirements — a dynamic similar to how California's CCPA became a de facto national privacy standard. However, Trump's EO 14365 (December 2025) seeks to challenge this extraterritorial reach through the Commerce Clause.

compliance_and_enforcement.penalties: Penalties vary significantly by state. Colorado: up to $20,000 per violation per consumer/transaction under the Colorado Consumer Protection Act, with 60-day cure period before enforcement. California SB 53: up to $1 million per violation enforced by California AG. New York RAISE Act: up to $1 million for first violation, $3 million for subsequent violations. Illinois HB 3773: up to $5,000 per violation plus compensatory remedies (back pay, reinstatement, emotional distress damages, attorneys' fees). Texas TRAIGA: civil penalties enforced by Texas AG (amount to be determined by rulemaking). Utah: up to $2,500 per administrative violation, $5,000 per court/administrative order violation. Notable: no state law currently includes criminal penalties for AI-related violations. Most states do not provide a private right of action — enforcement is typically reserved for state attorneys general.
compliance_and_enforcement.enforcement_body: All major state AI laws grant exclusive enforcement authority to the state attorney general, with some variations. Colorado: AG has exclusive enforcement and rulemaking authority. California: AG enforces SB 53. Illinois: Department of Human Rights enforces HB 3773 (employees can file charges). Texas: AG has exclusive enforcement, plus an online complaint mechanism. Utah: Division of Consumer Protection and AG. New York: AG enforces the RAISE Act, with oversight office within the Department of Financial Services publishing annual reports. No state has created a dedicated AI regulatory agency comparable to the EU AI Office.
compliance_and_enforcement.compliance_timeline: Key compliance deadlines (as of February 2026): ALREADY IN EFFECT: Utah AI Policy Act (May 1, 2024), Illinois HB 3773 (January 1, 2026), Texas TRAIGA (January 1, 2026), California SB 53 (January 1, 2026). UPCOMING: Colorado SB 24-205 (June 30, 2026 — delayed from February 1, 2026 to allow further legislative consideration), New York RAISE Act (January 1, 2027). PENDING: Colorado's 2026 regular legislative session (January-May 2026) may adopt substantive amendments to SB 24-205. New York chapter amendments expected to finalize the RAISE Act's revenue-based threshold. Multiple states considering new comprehensive AI bills in 2026 sessions (Connecticut, Virginia, Massachusetts, New Mexico tracking Colorado's model).
compliance_and_enforcement.reporting_requirements: Colorado: developers must provide deployers with system documentation; deployers must complete annual impact assessments and make them available on request. California SB 53: frontier developers must publish transparency reports, report critical safety incidents to regulators within 15 days, and (beginning 2027) the AG publishes anonymized annual whistleblower activity reports. New York RAISE Act: developers must report incidents to the state within 72 hours. Texas: government entities must disclose AI interactions. Illinois: employers must provide notice to employees/applicants when AI is used in employment decisions; IDHR draft rules specify recordkeeping requirements. Utah: disclosure upon consumer request (proactive for regulated professions).
compliance_and_enforcement.sme_provisions: Limited explicit SME provisions across states. Colorado includes a small business deployer exemption: deployers with fewer than 50 full-time employees who do not train the AI system on their own data and use it only for its intended purpose receive reduced obligations. Colorado also provides a rebuttable presumption of reasonable care for compliant entities, which helps SMEs demonstrate compliance. California SB 53's compute threshold (>10^26 FLOPS) effectively exempts all SMEs, as only a handful of large labs train models at that scale. Texas TRAIGA's regulatory sandbox is available to companies of any size, providing a controlled environment for testing AI systems without full regulatory exposure. New York RAISE Act's $500 million revenue threshold exempts SMEs entirely. Utah's regulatory sandbox is similarly available to startups. However, no state has implemented EU-style SME fee waivers, reduced documentation requirements, or delayed timelines specifically for small businesses. The patchwork itself disproportionately burdens SMEs that lack resources for multi-state compliance.
compliance_and_enforcement.liability_model: Varies by state. Colorado: fault_based — requires showing failure to exercise 'reasonable care' with rebuttable presumption for compliant entities; violations treated as deceptive trade practices. Illinois: reversed_burden_of_proof for disparate impact claims — employer must demonstrate AI system does not discriminate once disparate impact is shown, consistent with existing IHRA framework. Texas: fault_based with intent requirement — 'intentionally designed' standard means disparate impact alone is insufficient; safe_harbor for NIST AI RMF compliance. California SB 53: fault_based — civil penalties for failure to comply with safety, transparency, and reporting obligations. New York RAISE Act: fault_based — penalties for failure to submit reports or making false statements. Utah: fault_based — standard consumer protection enforcement. No state has adopted strict liability for AI harms.

impact_and_analysis.business_impact: LARGE ENTERPRISES: Face the highest absolute compliance costs but have resources to manage multi-state compliance. Companies like Google, Microsoft, Meta, OpenAI, and Anthropic must comply with the union of all state requirements since they operate nationally. This creates a de facto national standard set by the strictest state (currently Colorado for algorithmic discrimination, California for frontier model safety). Large enterprises are investing in AI governance teams, compliance tooling, and impact assessment processes. Some industry estimates suggest compliance adds ~17% overhead to AI system expenses. STARTUPS AND SMEs: Disproportionately burdened by the patchwork. The US Chamber of Commerce reports that California privacy and cybersecurity requirements alone impose ~$16,000 in annual compliance costs on small businesses. Multi-state compliance requires legal expertise most startups cannot afford. A 2024 US Chamber survey found 25% of small businesses not using AI cite legal/compliance concerns. However, several states include SME-friendly thresholds: California SB 53 and NY RAISE Act's compute/revenue thresholds effectively exempt startups; Colorado's small deployer exemption reduces obligations for companies under 50 employees. The Common Sense Institute projects Colorado's SB 24-205 will cost the state 40,000 jobs and $7 billion in economic output by 2030 (industry-funded study, disputed by consumer advocates). AI GOVERNANCE/COMPLIANCE INDUSTRY: The patchwork creates significant demand for compliance-as-a-service, AI auditing, bias testing, and legal advisory services. Companies like TrustArc, OneTrust, and specialized AI audit firms are expanding offerings. However, Trump's EO 14365 threatens this market by seeking to eliminate state-level requirements. SECTOR-SPECIFIC IMPACTS: Employment AI laws (Illinois, Colorado, NYC Local Law 144) most directly affect HR tech companies and hiring platforms. Healthcare AI regulations affect healthtech startups. Financial services AI rules add to existing regulatory burden from federal banking regulators.
impact_and_analysis.innovation_effect: Mixed and contested. PRO-INNOVATION ARGUMENTS: Safe harbors (Texas NIST AI RMF compliance, Colorado's rebuttable presumption) incentivize adoption of responsible AI practices without penalizing innovation. Regulatory sandboxes (Texas, Utah) allow experimentation in controlled environments. Clear rules reduce legal uncertainty that deters investment. ANTI-INNOVATION ARGUMENTS: The patchwork creates regulatory fragmentation that increases costs and slows deployment timelines. Definitional inconsistencies across states (different meanings of 'AI system,' 'high-risk,' 'consequential decision') force companies to maintain parallel compliance programs. Impact assessment requirements (Colorado) add time and cost to AI deployment cycles. The US Chamber of Commerce and tech industry groups argue the patchwork is more harmful than a single comprehensive federal law would be. EMPIRICAL EVIDENCE: The AI startup ecosystem in the US continues to attract the majority of global AI venture capital despite the patchwork, suggesting regulatory burden has not yet materially deterred investment. However, some startups report delaying product launches or avoiding certain state markets to minimize regulatory exposure.
impact_and_analysis.global_influence: The US state patchwork serves as both a cautionary tale and a model for other jurisdictions. CAUTIONARY TALE: The fragmentation illustrates the risks of sector-specific, jurisdiction-level regulation without federal coordination — a problem the EU explicitly sought to avoid with the AI Act's horizontal approach. Other countries (Canada, Australia, Japan) have cited the US patchwork as motivation for national-level AI frameworks. TEMPLATE EFFECT: Colorado's SB 24-205 is emerging as a template for other US states, with Connecticut, Massachusetts, New Mexico, New York, and Virginia considering bills tracking its framework. California's SB 53 and New York's RAISE Act together create a bicoastal standard for frontier model regulation that may become a de facto global template for frontier AI safety governance. REGULATORY COMPETITION: The interplay between state activism and federal deregulation (EO 14365) creates a dynamic tension that other federal systems (e.g., EU member states, Australian states) are watching. The outcome — whether federal preemption prevails or states retain regulatory authority — will influence how other federal jurisdictions approach AI governance.
impact_and_analysis.stakeholder_positions: INDUSTRY/PRO-INNOVATION: The US Chamber of Commerce strongly opposes the patchwork, arguing it stifles small business AI adoption and costs jobs. Tech industry trade groups (TechNet, Chamber Technology Engagement Center, ACT-The App Association) advocate for a single federal framework. Major AI labs (OpenAI, Google, Anthropic) generally prefer lighter-touch federal regulation to the current state patchwork. The Trump administration explicitly frames state AI regulation as a barrier to US global AI dominance. CONSUMER/CIVIL RIGHTS ADVOCATES: The Center for Democracy and Technology supports Colorado's SB 24-205 as a model for algorithmic accountability. The ACLU and civil rights organizations support state laws addressing AI discrimination, particularly in employment and housing. The Electronic Frontier Foundation has raised concerns about some state laws being too narrowly focused. Consumer groups argue that in the absence of federal action, state laws are the only available protection. STATE LEGISLATORS: Bipartisan support exists for state AI regulation — Colorado's SB 24-205 passed with both Democratic and Republican sponsors. State attorneys general (through NAAG) have published supportive analyses. However, some states (notably Texas) have taken more innovation-friendly approaches with intent-based liability and safe harbors. ACADEMIC/POLICY: The Future of Privacy Forum (FPF), IAPP, and Brookings Institution have published detailed analyses generally supporting thoughtful state regulation while acknowledging the patchwork problem.
impact_and_analysis.deregulatory_signals: Strong deregulatory signals at the federal level, mixed signals at the state level. FEDERAL: Trump's EO 14365 (December 2025) explicitly targets state AI laws, establishing a DOJ AI Litigation Task Force to challenge 'onerous' state laws, conditioning BEAD broadband funding on states not enforcing conflicting AI laws, and directing FTC/FCC to issue preemptive federal standards. Colorado's SB 24-205 is explicitly named as an example of a problematic law. STATE-LEVEL: Colorado delayed its own law from February to June 2026, with Governor Polis convening an AI Policy Working Group to consider amendments that might satisfy federal requirements. Virginia's comprehensive AI bill was vetoed by the governor in 2025. Several ambitious state bills were significantly weakened during legislative processes (e.g., California's original SB 1047 in 2024 was vetoed; the replacement SB 53 is narrower). However, New York moved forward with the RAISE Act despite federal opposition, and Illinois' employment AI law took effect on schedule. The net trajectory is uncertain: states continue legislating aggressively (1,200+ bills in 2025) while facing unprecedented federal pushback.

teaching_relevance.entrepreneurial_implications: CRITICAL COMPLIANCE LANDSCAPE FOR AI STARTUPS: (1) Multi-state compliance burden: Any AI startup serving customers across US states faces overlapping obligations — algorithmic discrimination prevention (Colorado), employment AI notice requirements (Illinois), frontier model safety (California, New York), prohibited uses (Texas), and basic disclosure (Utah). This creates a compliance burden that industry estimates at ~17% overhead on AI system costs. (2) Strategic threshold awareness: California SB 53 (>10^26 FLOPS) and NY RAISE Act ($500M revenue) only affect the largest AI labs — most startups are exempt from frontier model requirements. Colorado's small deployer exemption (< 50 employees, no custom training) offers relief for early-stage companies. Texas safe harbors reward NIST AI RMF adoption. Startups should understand which laws actually apply to them versus which generate compliance anxiety. (3) Market access decisions: Startups must decide whether to comply with the strictest standard (becoming compliant everywhere) or to geofence services away from heavily regulated states. The de facto national standard set by Colorado/California may make the 'comply everywhere' approach more practical. (4) Competitive moats from compliance: Startups that proactively build bias testing, impact assessment, and transparency capabilities gain a competitive advantage in B2B sales to enterprises that require AI governance from their vendors. 'Responsible AI' as a product differentiator works particularly well when selling to regulated industries (finance, healthcare, HR). (5) Regulatory uncertainty: The federal-state tension (EO 14365 vs. state laws) creates planning challenges. Prudent startups should continue complying with state laws while monitoring the federal framework development. Over-investing in compliance with laws that may be preempted is a risk, but abandoning responsible AI practices would be a bigger one. (6) EU contrast: The US patchwork vs. EU AI Act comparison is a key decision factor for startups choosing which market to prioritize. EU compliance (one framework, high cost) vs. US compliance (50 frameworks, fragmented but many exemptions for small companies) presents a genuine strategic tradeoff. (7) Compliance-as-a-service opportunity: The patchwork creates a market for AI governance SaaS — bias auditing, impact assessment automation, multi-state compliance dashboards — that entrepreneurial students might consider building. (8) For French/European entrepreneurs entering the US: understanding the patchwork is essential for market entry strategy — which states to target first, which compliance obligations to prioritize, and how the federal preemption battle may simplify or complicate the landscape.
teaching_relevance.session_mapping: Session 5 (Ethics, governance & final presentations) — primary: comparison of US patchwork vs. EU AI Act approaches to AI governance, state-federal tension, regulatory philosophy differences. Session 4 (AI business models & strategy) — secondary: compliance costs as business factor, regulatory moats, market access strategy across jurisdictions. Session 3 (Framing & managing AI projects) — tertiary: impact assessments, risk management requirements (Colorado), and how regulatory requirements should inform AI project planning and Build vs. Buy decisions.

confidence.caveats: RAPIDLY EVOLVING LANDSCAPE: This is the most dynamic area of AI regulation globally as of February 2026. Key uncertainties: (1) Colorado's 2026 legislative session (January-May) may substantially amend SB 24-205 before its June 30 effective date, potentially weakening its algorithmic discrimination provisions to satisfy federal requirements under EO 14365. (2) The Commerce Department evaluation of state AI laws due March 11, 2026 will determine which state laws are officially designated 'onerous' and targeted for federal challenge. (3) The DOJ AI Litigation Task Force may file lawsuits against state laws at any time, creating constitutional uncertainty that won't be resolved for months or years. (4) Congressional action on a comprehensive federal AI framework could preempt all state laws, but no bill has advanced significantly as of early 2026. (5) The 2026 state legislative sessions are expected to introduce hundreds of new AI bills, further expanding the patchwork. (6) The Common Sense Institute's economic impact estimates ($7B cost, 40,000 jobs lost from Colorado's law) are industry-funded and disputed by consumer advocates — these figures should be treated as advocacy data, not independent analysis. (7) State-level definitions of key terms ('AI system,' 'high-risk,' 'consequential decision,' 'developer,' 'deployer') are inconsistent and may evolve through rulemaking and case law.
